Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
event.description:
Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material.

Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions. Institutional Seat (2022) modifies a standard bench from the museum’s galleries into a version that is more comfortable for all museum visitors. Surround Sound (2022) attends to the floor of the gallery with dance-floor materials. Over the course of the exhibition, this floor will collect marks made by visitors’ shoes, strollers, and wheelchair treads, like another form of tally or notation.

Carolyn Lazard (b. 1987) is a New York-based artist whose primary medium is iteration. They also work across video, sculpture, installation, and performance. Their practice remembers the generative incapacity of debility.

Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is organized by the Cantor Arts Center, presenting work originally co-commissioned by the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis; the Institute of Contemporary Art, University of Pennsylvania; and Nottingham Contemporary, and is curated by Christina Linden, Director of Academic and Public Programs. We gratefully acknowledge support from The Lynn Krywick Gibbons Gallery Exhibitions Fund at the Cantor Arts Center.

event.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess  and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
event.description:
Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

From her elegant French gowns to a colossal painting of her jewels, from the Egyptian artifacts she acquired for her fledgling museum to a Hawaiian skirt she may or may not have purchased immediately before her suspicious death, Jane! presents various idiosyncratic artifacts of Stanford lore—many shown for the very first time, and very likely for the last.

IMAGE: Napoleon T. Sarony, Portrait of Jane Lathrop Stanford, 1871. Photograph with charcoal touch up, 55 ½ x 45 in. Cantor Arts Center, Stanford University, Stanford Family Collections, JLS.18217

event.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
event.description:
Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France. Though commercially unsuccessful, these experiments laid the groundwork for the scanning, machining, and printing technologies ubiquitous today. Bringing together these rare artifacts, the exhibition opens up a little-known chapter of history to reveal the roots and richness of our contemporary world. An accompanying catalogue features four newly commissioned essays accompanied by previously unpublished documentation, deepening our understanding of this overlooked chapter in the history of art and technology.

Image: François Willème (French, 1830–1905). Unfinished photosculpture bust, ca. 1860. Oak and twine on base. Gift of Eastman Kodak Company, ex-collection Gabriel Cromer, 1985.0517.0001. Courtesy of the George Eastman Museum

Diane Christensen Fund for African Art, The Halperin Exhibitions Fund, The Hockwald Fund, The Kazak Acquisitions and Exhibitions Fund, and The Robert Mondavi Family Fund.

event.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
event.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition.

event.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
event.description:
Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. 

Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century.  If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. 

Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. 

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford draws upon the extensive array of commercial almanacs, prints, postcards, commercial ephemera, stereographs, manuscripts, historic photographs, and other items that are a part of the Roxane Debuisson Collection of Paris history, circa 1789-1970, acquired by the Department of Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries in 2020. These materials place Paris as the birthplace of political, commercial, and urban innovations, and as a city defined by the tension between its historical past and its continuous reinvention. The exhibit highlights the city’s rapid changes and their diverse causes, while suggesting the collection’s vast possibilities for both research and instruction.

This exhibition is curated by Sarah Sussman, Assistant University Librarian for Collections and Services & Curator of French and Italian Collections, Stanford University Libraries, and Chloe Summers Edmondson, Assistant Professor of French at the University of Miami. Produced and designed by Deardra Fuzzell, with assistance from Kylee Jo Diedrich, Sofia McGullam Ornelas, and Pasha Tope.

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford will be open to the public. Registration at the entrance with a valid government ID is required to enter the Cecil H. Green Library and view the exhibit.

event.title: In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection
event.description:
In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection showcases recent acquisitions made through the Cantor’s Asian American Art Initiative (AAAI), offering a glimpse into one of the fastest-growing areas of the museum’s collection. Many of the works on view are being presented for the first time.

Founded in 2018 by Stanford art history professor Marci Kwon and Cantor associate curator of modern and contemporary art Aleesa Pitchamarn Alexander, the AAAI is one of the nation's leading museum initiatives dedicated to Asian American art. What began with approximately 30 works by Asian American artists has grown to more than 800 through acquisitions, exhibitions, publications, archival research, and community collaboration.

Rather than presenting a single definition of Asian American art, In Focus highlights its remarkable breadth. Spanning generations, media, and artistic approaches, the exhibition brings together works by artists of Asian descent working in the United States whose practices reflect a wide range of histories, perspectives, and creative concerns. Featuring works by Pacita Abad, Ching Ho Cheng, Tseng Kwong Chi, Young Joon Kwak, Masami Teraoka, and Rupy C. Tut, among others.

IMAGE: Pacita Abad (American, born in the Philippines, 1946–2004), If My Friends Could See Me Now, 1993. Lithograph with pulp-painted chine-collé and metallic powder on handmade paper. Cantor Arts Center, Stanford University. Robert E. and Mary B. P. Gross Fund, 2023.113. © Pacita Abad Art Estate LLC

event.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
event.room_number: Bowes Art & Architecture Library, 2nd floor. Visitors: Please call 650-723-3408 for building/elevator access.
event.description:
Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet.

Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm.

event.description:

About the Morton Feldman Centenary at Stanford:
In celebration of the centenary of the American composer Morton Feldman (1926 –1987), the Stanford Symposium on Music and the Brain, The Department of Music, the Center for Computer Research in Music and Acoustics, and the Anderson Collection at Stanford University present a program examining the decades-long aesthetic dialogue between Feldman and the painters of the New York School. Throughout his career, Feldman enjoyed close friendships with artists including Mark Rothko, Philip Guston, Robert Rauschenberg, Jasper Johns, and Willem de Kooning. Feldman’s music, like the works of these artists, concerns abstract patterns, subtle variations, surface, materiality, and scale.

New York City’s BlackBox Ensemble will be performing works of Feldman’s alongside responses by Stanford composers Jonathan Berger, Erik Ulman, Lemon Guo, Calvin Van Zytveld, Celeste Betancur and Brian Brown across two concerts. The first concert takes place at Stanford’s Anderson collection, where the music of Feldman can be heard amidst paintings of Feldman’s friends. The second concert will take place at the CCRMA (Center for Computer Research in Music and Acoustics) Stage. These concerts are part of a symposium Stopping time: How music alters time perception and will include public lectures providing perspectives on Feldman’s unique temporal world, and the psychology and neuroscience of durational artistic experiences.

event.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
event.description:
Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material.

Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions. Institutional Seat (2022) modifies a standard bench from the museum’s galleries into a version that is more comfortable for all museum visitors. Surround Sound (2022) attends to the floor of the gallery with dance-floor materials. Over the course of the exhibition, this floor will collect marks made by visitors’ shoes, strollers, and wheelchair treads, like another form of tally or notation.

Carolyn Lazard (b. 1987) is a New York-based artist whose primary medium is iteration. They also work across video, sculpture, installation, and performance. Their practice remembers the generative incapacity of debility.

Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is organized by the Cantor Arts Center, presenting work originally co-commissioned by the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis; the Institute of Contemporary Art, University of Pennsylvania; and Nottingham Contemporary, and is curated by Christina Linden, Director of Academic and Public Programs. We gratefully acknowledge support from The Lynn Krywick Gibbons Gallery Exhibitions Fund at the Cantor Arts Center.

event.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess  and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
event.description:
Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

From her elegant French gowns to a colossal painting of her jewels, from the Egyptian artifacts she acquired for her fledgling museum to a Hawaiian skirt she may or may not have purchased immediately before her suspicious death, Jane! presents various idiosyncratic artifacts of Stanford lore—many shown for the very first time, and very likely for the last.

IMAGE: Napoleon T. Sarony, Portrait of Jane Lathrop Stanford, 1871. Photograph with charcoal touch up, 55 ½ x 45 in. Cantor Arts Center, Stanford University, Stanford Family Collections, JLS.18217

event.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
event.description:
Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France. Though commercially unsuccessful, these experiments laid the groundwork for the scanning, machining, and printing technologies ubiquitous today. Bringing together these rare artifacts, the exhibition opens up a little-known chapter of history to reveal the roots and richness of our contemporary world. An accompanying catalogue features four newly commissioned essays accompanied by previously unpublished documentation, deepening our understanding of this overlooked chapter in the history of art and technology.

Image: François Willème (French, 1830–1905). Unfinished photosculpture bust, ca. 1860. Oak and twine on base. Gift of Eastman Kodak Company, ex-collection Gabriel Cromer, 1985.0517.0001. Courtesy of the George Eastman Museum

event.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
event.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition.

event.description:
Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet.

Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm.

event.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
event.description:
Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. 

Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century.  If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. 

Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. 

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford draws upon the extensive array of commercial almanacs, prints, postcards, commercial ephemera, stereographs, manuscripts, historic photographs, and other items that are a part of the Roxane Debuisson Collection of Paris history, circa 1789-1970, acquired by the Department of Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries in 2020. These materials place Paris as the birthplace of political, commercial, and urban innovations, and as a city defined by the tension between its historical past and its continuous reinvention. The exhibit highlights the city’s rapid changes and their diverse causes, while suggesting the collection’s vast possibilities for both research and instruction.

This exhibition is curated by Sarah Sussman, Assistant University Librarian for Collections and Services & Curator of French and Italian Collections, Stanford University Libraries, and Chloe Summers Edmondson, Assistant Professor of French at the University of Miami. Produced and designed by Deardra Fuzzell, with assistance from Kylee Jo Diedrich, Sofia McGullam Ornelas, and Pasha Tope.

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford will be open to the public. Registration at the entrance with a valid government ID is required to enter the Cecil H. Green Library and view the exhibit.

event.title: In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection
event.description:
In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection showcases recent acquisitions made through the Cantor’s Asian American Art Initiative (AAAI), offering a glimpse into one of the fastest-growing areas of the museum’s collection. Many of the works on view are being presented for the first time.

Founded in 2018 by Stanford art history professor Marci Kwon and Cantor associate curator of modern and contemporary art Aleesa Pitchamarn Alexander, the AAAI is one of the nation's leading museum initiatives dedicated to Asian American art. What began with approximately 30 works by Asian American artists has grown to more than 800 through acquisitions, exhibitions, publications, archival research, and community collaboration.

Rather than presenting a single definition of Asian American art, In Focus highlights its remarkable breadth. Spanning generations, media, and artistic approaches, the exhibition brings together works by artists of Asian descent working in the United States whose practices reflect a wide range of histories, perspectives, and creative concerns. Featuring works by Pacita Abad, Ching Ho Cheng, Tseng Kwong Chi, Young Joon Kwak, Masami Teraoka, and Rupy C. Tut, among others.

event.title: CEE PhD Defense: Eleanor Ho, "A Multi-Scale Investigation of Building Energy Use: From Attribution to Prediction, for Design and Operational Decision-Making"
event.description:
Abstract:

Buildings account for roughly one third of global energy use, and both their design and operation shape how much they consume. This dissertation investigates building energy use across spatial scales, asking how building and urban form attributes affect energy use, and at what level of modeling detail we can support design and operational decisions. At the urban scale, an empirical study of hourly smart meter data from 170,224 utility customers shows that population density has significant, non-linear, and size-dependent effects on building energy use intensity, with reductions of up to 32-74% per density level across building types, consistent across monthly, daily, and hourly scales. At the fleet scale, the analysis moves from a static snapshot to time-varying attribution, asking which external drivers a building's energy use is coupled to and how that dependency structure evolves over time, by applying time-varying graphical lasso to metered electricity and open data for a fleet of buildings. Results across ten temporal lenses show that the dominant driver depends on the lens itself: solar and traffic dominate at daily and sub-daily resolution, and temperature emerges at hourly resolution when days of the same month are merged. At the building scale, a single multi-zone campus building and a controlled temperature setback experiment serve as one testbed for asking whether a physics-based model can predict a building's response to operational changes, and how much physics that takes. An EnergyPlus model calibrated against the measured setback response first shows that it can, reproducing the building's response to setpoint changes and evaluating operational strategies before implementation. The dissertation then asks how much of that physics is enough: a hybrid model combining an uncalibrated EnergyPlus simulation with downstream machine learning predicts cooling loads under unseen temperature setbacks within ASHRAE Guideline 14 tolerances, while pure machine learning baselines fall short without weeks of measured data from the new regime. This enables portfolio-scale deployment without demanding costly per-building calibration or field experiments. Together, these studies move from quantifying magnitude, to attributing drivers, to prediction, in support of design and operational decision-making.

At the building scale, a single multi-zone campus building and a controlled temperature setback experiment serve as one testbed for asking whether a physics-based model can predict a building's response to operational changes, and how much physics that takes. An EnergyPlus model calibrated against the measured setback response first shows that it can, reproducing the building's response to setpoint changes and evaluating operational strategies before implementation. The dissertation then asks how much of that physics is enough: a hybrid model combining an uncalibrated EnergyPlus simulation with downstream machine learning predicts cooling loads under unseen temperature setbacks within ASHRAE Guideline 14 tolerances, while pure machine learning baselines fall short without weeks of measured data from the new regime. This enables portfolio-scale deployment without demanding costly per-building calibration or field experiments. Together, these studies move from quantifying magnitude, to attributing drivers, to prediction, in support of design and operational decision-making.

event.room_number: James Lin and Nisa Leung Seminar Room, E153
event.description:
Understanding Vision Through Neural Supervision and Generative Probes

Abstract

How can neural data guide the learning of visual representations, and how can we choose stimuli that reveal their properties? I will present two lines of work addressing these questions. First, I will show how training a model to emulate V4 responses yields visual representations that capture multiple signatures of human perception, often better than task-optimized models, highlighting what biological supervision contributes beyond task-based training. Second, I will introduce diffusion models as stimulus engines for probing sensitivity in biological and artificial visual systems. We use the local geometry of a learned natural-image distribution to construct controlled image perturbations, revealing a systematic relationship between density curvature and human and model sensitivity. This approach makes the choice of where to probe stimulus space an explicit part of understanding and comparing visual representations. Together, these directions point toward a productive exchange between neuroscience and AI: neural data can guide more human-like models, while generative models open new avenues for discovering how biological and artificial visual systems represent the world.


Meenakshi Khosla
 

UC San Diego, Department of Cognitive Science


Meenakshi Khosla is an Assistant Professor of Cognitive Science at UC San Diego, with an affiliate appointment in Computer Science and Engineering. Her research at the intersection of computational neuroscience and machine learning aims to understand how brains and artificial neural networks represent information and how these representations support perception and cognition. She received her Ph.D. in Electrical and Computer Engineering from Cornell University and was an ICoN Postdoctoral Fellow at MIT. Her research is supported by the Kavli Institute for Brain and Mind, Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), and NSF’s Collaborative Research in Computational Neuroscience grants.

event.title: Unpacking the Trump - Xi Meeting: What Happened and What's Next?
event.description:
Drawing on decades of experience at the center of U.S. policy toward China, Mark Lambert, former State Department China Coordinator and recently appointed China Policy Fellow at Stanford’s Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC), and Ambassador Laura Stone, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for China and Mongolia and currently affiliated with Stanford’s Center for East Asian Studies, offer an insider’s assessment of the Trump-Xi state visit and its implications for U.S.-China relations.

Lambert and Stone will examine what Washington and Beijing each sought from the visit, what the two leaders actually achieved, and what the agreements, rhetoric, and notable omissions reveal about the state of the relationship. They will assess the implications for trade and economic ties, Taiwan and regional security, strategic competition, and the prospects for managing tensions between the world’s two most powerful countries. Please join us for a candid discussion of what the state visit changed, what it did not, and where U.S.-China relations may be headed next.

Speakers: 

Mark Lambert is the China Policy Fellow at Stanford University’s Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC). A career U.S. diplomat and one of the State Department’s leading China experts, he most recently served as Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for China and Taiwan and as the Department’s China Coordinator. Over the course of his Foreign Service career, Lambert held senior positions focused on China, East Asia, and international organizations, including multiple assignments in Beijing. He also served as a senior advisor in the Bureau of International Organization Affairs, where his work focused on China’s role in the United Nations and other multilateral institutions.

Ambassador Laura Stone is affiliated with Stanford University’s Center for East Asian Studies. A career member of the Senior Foreign Service, she most recently served as U.S. Ambassador to the Republic of the Marshall Islands. Previously, she served as Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for China and Mongolia, with responsibility for managing U.S.-China relations during the Obama and first Trump administrations, and as Deputy Assistant Secretary for South Asia. Her other senior positions include Director of the Office of Chinese and Mongolian Affairs, Director of the State Department’s Office of Economic Policy in the Bureau of East Asian and Pacific Affairs, and Economic Counselor in Hanoi. She served three tours at the U.S. Embassy in Beijing and has spent more than three decades working on U.S. policy toward China and the Indo-Pacific.

event.title: Stanford Energy Seminar | AI for Climate Solutions: GRAIL | Shanthakumar Bannirchelvam, SUN New Energy Capital
event.description:
The Stanford Energy Seminar has been a mainstay of energy engagement at Stanford for nearly 20 years and is one of the flagship programs of the Precourt Institute for Energy. We aim to bring a wide variety of perspectives to the Stanford community – academics, entrepreneurs, utilities, non-profits, and more. 

About the talk

GRAIL — the Green Artificial Intelligence Learning network — is a global collaboration platform, founded by the Nand & Jeet Khemka Foundation, built to close the gap between two communities that rarely work together: the people building frontier AI and the people running the climate systems that need to decarbonise. Promising AI capability too often fails to convert into deployed outcomes because there is no translation layer between them. GRAIL is that layer to bring AI solutions to transform applied domains including energy, materials, value chains and the built environment to create economic value and deliver climate impact.

Shanthakumar Bannirchelvam is a Director of the Sustainable and AI investing teams at the SUN Group, a 120-year-old business group and Single Family Office which has established leading asset managers including Sequoia Capital India (now Peak XV Partners). Prior to this role, he worked at Nomura Greentech in their sustainable investment banking division, where he advised on infrastructure and energy transition deals.

He has also previously worked in corporate law in Sydney and London with Herbert Smith Freehills, the United Nations Economic and Social Council in New York and served as an Infantry Officer in the Singapore Armed Forces. Shanthakumar is admitted to practice in the Supreme Court of NSW and holds a Bachelor of Laws / Bachelor of Economics from the University of Sydney and an MBA from Columbia Business School, where he was a Three Cairns Climate Fellow.

 

Anyone with an interest in energy is welcome to join! You can enjoy seminars in the following ways:

  • Attend live. The auditorium may change quarter by quarter, so check each seminar event to confirm the location. Explore the current quarter's schedule.
  • Watch live in a browser livestream if available. Check each seminar event for its unique livestream URL.

event.description:
The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future.

The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist.

The exhibition is curated by Jee-Young Park, Korean Studies Librarian, and Jisoo Kim, an SFSU MA Museum Studies graduate and San Francisco-based curator.

event.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
event.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition.

event.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
event.description:
Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. 

Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century.  If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. 

Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. 

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford draws upon the extensive array of commercial almanacs, prints, postcards, commercial ephemera, stereographs, manuscripts, historic photographs, and other items that are a part of the Roxane Debuisson Collection of Paris history, circa 1789-1970, acquired by the Department of Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries in 2020. These materials place Paris as the birthplace of political, commercial, and urban innovations, and as a city defined by the tension between its historical past and its continuous reinvention. event.title: Cooking for Hormonal Wellness During Perimenopause
event.description:
Perimenopause can bring changes in sleep, energy, mood, body composition, and overall well-being. Although food cannot prevent the natural hormonal changes that occur during this stage of life, research suggests that dietary patterns and lifestyle choices can help manage symptoms and support long-term muscle, bone, brain, metabolic, and cardiovascular health.

Join us for a virtual cooking demonstration focused on creating satisfying, practical meals during perimenopause and menopause. Through recipes for breakfast, snacks, dinner, and dessert, you will learn how to incorporate protein, fiber, healthy fats, and plant foods in ways that support more balanced energy, blood sugar regulation, digestive health, and satiety.

While demonstrating the recipes and cooking techniques, we will share current research on food and lifestyle practices during midlife, as well as realistic strategies for building balanced meals, supporting muscle and bone health, and making nutritious choices easier during busy or low-energy days.

Ingredient substitutions, including a variety of protein options, will be demonstrated or suggested to accommodate most dietary needs and preferences. By the end of the session, you will have approachable recipes and practical strategies to support yourself or someone you care about through the menopausal transition and beyond.

This class will be recorded and a one-week link to the recording will be shared with all registered participants. 

To receive incentive points, attend at least 80% of the live session or listen to the entire recording within one week.

event.title: Earth & Planetary Sciences Seminar - Josh Goodwin, PG, CEG - “Geologist-in-Training (GIT): Pathway to the California Professional Geologist License.”
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 320, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description: The Board invites you to learn about certification as a Geologist-In-Training (GIT). The GIT is the first step toward becoming a California-licensed Professional Geologist (PG). Learn about the laws and regulations that govern the practice of geology in California and why being licensed is important to your future success as a geologist. Gain an understanding of important definitions in the Geologist and Geophysicist Act (Law), and how to get on-the-job experience in order to qualify for a geology license. Finding a job once you’ve got your degree can be a daunting prospect. Here’s your chance to get the perspective of a professional geologist on the entire career process (resume, interviews, job experience, licensure), and to learn how the GIT can give you credibility when applying for jobs.
